claim: Memories can reactivate during non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep.
source: It is now well established that memories can reactivate during non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep, but the question of whether equivalent reactivation can be detected in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is hotly debated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research and is presented as established scientific consensus.

claim: The question of whether equivalent reactivation can be detected in REM sleep is hotly debated.
source: It is now well established that memories can reactivate during non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep, but the question of whether equivalent reactivation can be detected in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is hotly debated.
evidence: This reflects the state of the scientific debate as characterized by the authors.

claim: Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) involves pairing sounds with learned material during wake and re-presenting them during subsequent sleep to trigger reactivation.
source: To examine this, we used a technique called targeted memory reactivation (TMR) in which sounds are paired with learned material in wake, and then re-presented in subsequent sleep, in this case REM, to trigger reactivation.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Machine learning classifiers can identify reactivation of task-related motor imagery from wake in REM sleep.
source: We then used machine learning classifiers to identify reactivation of task-related motor imagery from wake in REM sleep.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: The strength of measured reactivation positively predicted overnight performance improvement.
source: Interestingly, the strength of measured reactivation positively predicted overnight performance improvement.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's behavioral analysis.

claim: This study provides the first evidence for memory reactivation in human REM sleep after TMR that is directly related to brain activity during wakeful task performance.
source: These findings provide the first evidence for memory reactivation in human REM sleep after TMR that is directly related to brain activity during wakeful task performance.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the novelty of their findings.

claim: The reactivation of memories in non-REM sleep is widely supported by evidence from numerous species.
source: The reactivation of memories in non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep is widely supported by evidence from numerous species (Rasch and Born, 2013; Bendor and Wilson, 2012; Wang et al., 2019; Ji and Wilson, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The first evidence for non-REM reactivation came from rodents.
source: The first evidence for non-REM reactivation came from rodents (Pavlides and Winson, 1989; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994)
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical research.

claim: Memory reactivation has been identified in humans using EEG classifiers.
source: such reactivation has subsequently been identified in humans using EEG classifiers (Wang et al., 2019; Belal et al., 2018; Schreiner et al., 2018; Cairney et al., 2018; Abdellahi et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Memory reactivation has been identified in humans using fMRI.
source: such reactivation has subsequently been identified in humans using EEG classifiers (Wang et al., 2019; Belal et al., 2018; Schreiner et al., 2018; Cairney et al., 2018; Abdellahi et al., 2023), fMRI (Shanahan et al., 2018; Rasch et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Memory reactivation has been identified in humans using intracranial recordings.
source: such reactivation has subsequently been identified in humans using EEG classifiers (Wang et al., 2019; Belal et al., 2018; Schreiner et al., 2018; Cairney et al., 2018; Abdellahi et al., 2023), fMRI (Shanahan et al., 2018; Rasch et al., 2007), and intracranial recordings (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Only a few rodent studies have shown evidence for reactivation in REM sleep.
source: Only a few rodent studies have shown evidence for reactivation in REM sleep (Pavlides and Winson, 1989; Louie and Wilson, 2001; Hennevin et al., 1995; Poe et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Schönauer et al., 2017 used EEG classifiers to distinguish between REM sleep on nights after training on two very different tasks.
source: but support for such reactivation comes from human work by Schönauer et al., 2017, who used EEG classifiers to elegantly distinguish between the REM sleep on nights after training on two very different tasks.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The reinstatement of EEG activity in REM that directly relates to EEG activity during a task in wake has yet to be demonstrated in humans.
source: Nevertheless, the reinstatement of EEG activity in REM that directly relates to EEG activity during a task in wake has yet to be demonstrated in humans.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to the current study.

claim: TMR is linked to neural plasticity when applied in non-REM sleep.
source: Targeted memory reactivation (TMR), a technique which allows the active triggering of memory reactivation, is linked to both neural (Lewis and Bendor, 2019; Berkers et al., 2018) and behavioural (Hu et al., 2019; Pereira et al., 2022; Oudiette and Paller, 2013) plasticity when applied in non-REM sleep.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TMR is linked to behavioural plasticity when applied in non-REM sleep.
source: Targeted memory reactivation (TMR), a technique which allows the active triggering of memory reactivation, is linked to both neural (Lewis and Bendor, 2019; Berkers et al., 2018) and behavioural (Hu et al., 2019; Pereira et al., 2022; Oudiette and Paller, 2013) plasticity when applied in non-REM sleep.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TMR provides a temporal window for reactivation to occur as a result of the external cue.
source: TMR provides a temporal window for reactivation to occur as a result of the external cue, and this can be used to evaluate the detectability of such reactivation.
evidence: This is a methodological rationale based on the properties of TMR.

claim: Theta activity predominates during REM.
source: Given that theta activity predominates during REM (Lomas et al., 2015; Nishida et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The serial reaction time task (SRTT) is sleep sensitive.
source: We chose the serial reaction time task (SRTT), which is known to be sleep sensitive (Spencer et al., 2006; Born and Wilhelm, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The SRTT is modulated by TMR in non-REM sleep.
source: The SRTT is modulated by TMR in non-REM sleep (Cousins et al., 2014; Cousins et al., 2016; Rakowska et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The SRTT has been strongly linked to REM.
source: The SRTT is modulated by TMR in non-REM sleep (Cousins et al., 2014; Cousins et al., 2016; Rakowska et al., 2021) but has also been strongly linked to REM (Maquet et al., 2000; Peigneux et al., 2003; Laureys et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Brain areas activated during SRTT execution have been shown to reactivate during subsequent REM.
source: For instance, brain areas which were activated during the execution of an SRTT have been shown to reactivate during subsequent REM (Maquet et al., 2000; Peigneux et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Greater connectivity between premotor cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and bilateral pre-supplementary motor areas has been observed during REM after SRTT training.
source: Furthermore, greater connectivity between premotor cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and bilateral pre-supplementary motor areas has been observed during REM after training on this task (Laureys et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Participants were presented with audio-visual cues and responded by pressing four buttons in the SRTT.
source: In our SRTT, participants were presented with audio-visual cues and responded by pressing four buttons (two with each hand), visual cues are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and references a figure.

claim: The cues in the SRTT were organised into an implicit 12-item sequence which was practiced repeatedly.
source: These cues were organised into an implicit 12-item sequence which was practiced repeatedly.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The cue-sounds were replayed during subsequent REM sleep to trigger the associated memories of left- and right-hand presses.
source: The cue-sounds were then replayed during subsequent REM sleep to trigger the associated memories of left- and right-hand presses (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and references a figure.

claim: Participants were trained on two sequences and only one was replayed in sleep.
source: We trained participants on two sequences and replayed only one of them in sleep.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: An adaptation night was included in which participants slept in the lab and the same cue-sounds were played during sleep before being paired with any memory.
source: As a control, we included an adaptation night in which participants slept in the lab and we played the same cue-sounds that would later be played during the experimental night.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: A null finding from the adaptation night would ensure that the study is decoding actual memories, not just sounds.
source: This provided an important control, as a null finding from this adaptation night would ensure that we are decoding actual memories, not just sounds.
evidence: This is a methodological rationale.

claim: Linear classification on EEGs during REM sleep was used to discriminate between neural reactivation of left- and right-hand button presses.
source: We used these data to discriminate between neural reactivation of left- and right-hand button presses using linear classification on EEGs during REM sleep, see Methods for more details.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: The EEG response showed a rapid increase in theta band followed by an increase in beta band starting about 1 s after TMR onset.
source: As shown in Figure 2a, the EEG response showed a rapid increase in theta band followed by an increase in beta band starting about 1 s after TMR onset.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-frequency analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: REM sleep is dominated by theta activity, which is thought to support the consolidation process.
source: REM sleep is dominated by theta activity, which is thought to support the consolidation process (Diekelmann and Born, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Increased theta power has previously been shown to occur after successful cueing during sleep.
source: and increased theta power has previously been shown to occur after successful cueing during sleep (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Theta was significantly higher in the first second post-TMR onset than in the baseline period for the adaptation night.
source: Focussing on the first second post-TMR onset, we found that theta was significantly higher here than in the baseline period, prior to the cue [-300 -100]ms, for both adaptation (Wilcoxon signed rank test, n=14, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: Theta was significantly higher in the first second post-TMR onset than in the baseline period for the experimental night.
source: Focussing on the first second post-TMR onset, we found that theta was significantly higher here than in the baseline period, prior to the cue [-300 -100]ms, for both adaptation (Wilcoxon signed rank test, n=14, p<0.001) and experimental nights (Wilcoxon signed rank test, n=14, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: There was no difference in theta power between experimental and adaptation conditions.
source: The absence of any difference in theta power between experimental and adaptation conditions (Wilcoxon signed rank test, n=14, p=0.68) suggests that this response is related to processing of the sound cue itself, not to memory reactivation.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The theta response after TMR is related to processing of the sound cue itself, not to memory reactivation.
source: The absence of any difference in theta power between experimental and adaptation conditions (Wilcoxon signed rank test, n=14, p=0.68) suggests that this response is related to processing of the sound cue itself, not to memory reactivation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical finding.

claim: A small increase in ERP amplitude was found immediately after TMR onset, followed by a decrease in amplitude 500 ms after the cue.
source: Turning to the ERP analysis, we found a small increase in ERP amplitude immediately after TMR onset, followed by a decrease in amplitude 500 ms after the cue.
evidence: This is a finding from the ERP analysis.

claim: Comparison of ERPs from experimental and adaptation nights showed no significant difference.
source: Comparison of ERPs from experimental and adaptation nights showed no significant difference, (n=14, p>0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The ERPs observed relate to the processing of the sound cues rather than any associated memory.
source: Similar to the time-frequency result, this suggests that the ERPs observed here relate to the processing of the sound cues rather than any associated memory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical finding.

claim: Classification models were trained using sleep data and then tested on wake data.
source: We trained our EEG classification models using sleep data and then tested them on wake data.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: Training a classification model on wake could cause the model to weigh features which are dominant in wake very highly even if those features were absent from sleep.
source: We chose to do this because training a classification model on wake could cause the model to weigh features which are dominant in wake very highly even if those features were absent from sleep.
evidence: This is a methodological rationale.

claim: Training models on sleep data ensured that the features associated with reactivation were used by the models.
source: By training our models on sleep data, we ensured that the features associated with reactivation were used by the models, and the models were thus able to look for these in the stronger, less noisy, signals recorded during wake.
evidence: This is a methodological rationale.

claim: A searchlight approach was used to locate the channels of interest.
source: We used a searchlight approach to locate the channels of interest, see Methods for details.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: A linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier was used in a time × time classification procedure.
source: We then used a linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier in a time × time classification procedure (King and Dehaene, 2014).
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: The classification process was repeated using the adaptation night to ensure that the classification was not caused by sound-induced effect or EEG noise.
source: We also repeated the classification process using the adaptation night to be certain that the classification was not caused by sound-induced effect or EEG noise rather than reactivation of the encoded memory.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: Comparison of the experimental night to the adaptation night showed a significantly higher AUC for the experimental night around 1 s after the onset of the cue.
source: Comparison of the experimental night to the adaptation night showed a significantly higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for the experimental night, described by a cluster (n=14, p=0.004) around 1 s after the onset of the cue at time 0, Figure 2c.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: In the adaptation night, no significant classification strength was found compared to chance.
source: In the adaptation night, no significant classification strength was found compared to chance (AUC=0.5), demonstrating that classification of this control condition did not differ from chance level.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: Comparison of the experimental night against chance showed a significantly higher AUC around 1 s after the onset of the cue.
source: By contrast, comparison of the experimental night against chance showed a significantly higher AUC around 1 s after the onset of the cue for the experimental night, (n=14, p=0.009), Figure 2d.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Memory reactivation after TMR cues in REM sleep can be detected.
source: These findings are significant when evaluated against both control and chance level, clearly demonstrating that we can detect memory reactivation after TMR cues in REM sleep.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: TMR elicited an increase in theta power in both experimental and adaptation nights.
source: As described in the section above, TMR elicited an increase in theta power in both experimental and adaptation nights.
evidence: This refers back to a previous finding in the manuscript.

claim: Theta responses after TMR have been implicated in reactivation and consolidation.
source: Because theta responses after TMR have been implicated in reactivation and consolidation (Schreiner and Rasch, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Classification using only theta band did not differ from chance.
source: Interestingly, classification did not differ from chance in this theta-only analysis (p>0.3), suggesting that theta activity itself does not hold the information used to detect reactivation.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: Theta activity itself does not hold the information used to detect reactivation.
source: Interestingly, classification did not differ from chance in this theta-only analysis (p>0.3), suggesting that theta activity itself does not hold the information used to detect reactivation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical finding.

claim: Classification analysis with theta band filtered out showed a pattern of significant difference similar to that of the original classification.
source: For completeness, we also conducted a positive control in which we filtered out theta band and performed our classification analysis. We found a pattern of significant difference similar to that of the original classification in Figure 2c and d.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: There was a significant difference against chance level when theta band was filtered out.
source: Specifically, there was a significant difference against both chance level (n=14, p=0.007, corrected with cluster-based permutation) and the adaptation night (n=14, p=0.009, corrected with cluster-based permutation), as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a significant difference against the adaptation night when theta band was filtered out.
source: Specifically, there was a significant difference against both chance level (n=14, p=0.007, corrected with cluster-based permutation) and the adaptation night (n=14, p=0.009, corrected with cluster-based permutation), as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TMR in SWS leads to reliable behavioural benefits in the SRTT.
source: Because TMR in SWS leads to reliable behavioural benefits in the SRTT Cousins et al., 2014; Cousins et al., 2016
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Relative sequence improvement (cued vs un-cued) did not differ from chance.
source: Our examination of overnight change showed that relative sequence improvement (cued vs un-cued) did not differ from chance (Wilcoxon signed rank test, n=14, p=0.43), Figure 3a
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The null result regarding the impact of TMR mirrors the finding of Cousins et al., 2016, where there was no significant result of stimulation.
source: This null result regarding the impact of TMR mirrors the finding of Cousins et al., 2016, where there was no significant result of stimulation, but there was a correlation with sleep spindles, which are thought to be markers of reactivation.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research supported by a citation.

claim: There was a positive correlation between classification performance and relative sequence improvement.
source: This revealed a positive correlation (n=14, r=0.56, p=0.04), Figure 3b.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There was no significant correlation between classification performance and pre-sleep performance.
source: We therefore checked for a correlation between classification performance and pre-sleep performance to determine whether the degree of pre-sleep learning predicted the extent of reactivation, this showed no significant correlation (n=14, r=–0.39, p=0.17).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The extent to which reactivation can be detected in REM sleep predicted the extent to which sequence memory improves overnight.
source: Together, these findings suggest that while our TMR cueing did not lead to an overall significant benefit in behavioural performance, the extent to which we can detect reactivation in REM sleep did predict the extent to which sequence memory improves overnight, and this was not dependent on pre-sleep learning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical findings.

claim: The extent to which reactivation can be detected in REM sleep was not dependent on pre-sleep learning.
source: Together, these findings suggest that while our TMR cueing did not lead to an overall significant benefit in behavioural performance, the extent to which we can detect reactivation in REM sleep did predict the extent to which sequence memory improves overnight, and this was not dependent on pre-sleep learning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical findings.

claim: Memory reactivation after TMR cues in human REM sleep can be decoded using EEG classifiers.
source: In this paper we demonstrated that memory reactivation after TMR cues in human REM sleep can be decoded using EEG classifiers.
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their primary finding.

claim: Reactivation appears to be most prominent about 1 second after the sound cue onset.
source: Such reactivation appears to be most prominent about 1 second after the sound cue onset.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The theta response after TMR is related to the tone, and does not embody the reactivation in and of itself.
source: Interestingly, although TMR also elicited an increase in theta power, our data suggest that this response is related to the tone, and does not embody the reactivation in and of itself.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Detectable memory reactivation is temporally consistent among trials and participants.
source: Our data suggest that detectable memory reactivation is temporally consistent among trials and participants, as reflected in the timing of the clusters in Figure 2c and d.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: During wake, classification is more prominent around 0.6 s after the cue.
source: During wake, classification is more prominent around 0.6 s after the cue, whereas in REM it starts about 0.4 s later.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: In REM, classification starts about 0.4 s later than in wake.
source: During wake, classification is more prominent around 0.6 s after the cue, whereas in REM it starts about 0.4 s later.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The delayed start of classification in REM could potentially be due to the brain taking more time to process information and reactivate a memory during REM sleep than during wake.
source: This delayed start could potentially be due to the brain taking more time to process information and reactivate a memory during REM sleep than during wake.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding.

claim: Reactivation in SWS has been shown to be delayed, appearing approximately from 1 s to 4.5 s after cue onset in a task of associating spatial locations with left- and right-hand movements.
source: In fact, reactivation in SWS has also been shown to be delayed, appearing approximately from 1 s to 4.5 s after cue onset in a task of associating spatial locations with left- and right-hand movements (Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Reactivation in SWS has been shown to appear around 2 s after cue onset in a picture memory task.
source: around 2 s after cue onset in a picture memory task (Cairney et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Reactivation in SWS has been shown to appear up to 10 s after cue onset in rodents.
source: and up to 10 s after cue onset in rodents (Bendor and Wilson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Wakeful theta is associated with attention during wake.
source: REM sleep is dominated by theta activity, which is linked to attention during wake (Biel et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Theta is more prominent with higher executive control.
source: and is more prominent with higher executive control (Magosso et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Wakeful theta is associated with the encoding of new information and memory processing.
source: Wakeful theta is also associated with the encoding of new information and memory processing (Vertes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Studies in non-REM have shown that TMR triggers an increase in theta followed by an increase in sigma band.
source: Furthermore, studies in non-REM have shown that TMR triggers an increase in theta followed by an increase in sigma band (Cairney et al., 2018; Schechtman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TMR elicited a power increase in theta band in REM sleep irrespective of whether the cues are meaningful or not.
source: Our data are in keeping with this, as we show that TMR elicited a power increase in theta band in REM sleep irrespective of whether the cues are meaningful (experimental night) or not (control night).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The theta activity observed following TMR cues was related to the processing of the sound cues and not a representative of reactivation.
source: We therefore conclude that the theta activity we observed following TMR cues was related to the processing of the sound cues and not a representative of reactivation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis.

claim: The performance of REM classifiers positively predicts overnight improvement on sequence memory.
source: The performance of our REM classifiers positively predicts overnight improvement on sequence memory.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Similar correlations between classification performance and behaviour have been found in non-REM TMR.
source: Similar correlations between classification performance and behaviour have been found in non-REM TMR (Wang et al., 2019; Shanahan et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: More reactivation might mean more consolidation, and therefore better post-sleep performance.
source: This could lead to the speculation that more reactivation means more consolidation, and therefore better post-sleep performance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: TMR in REM sleep lead to no overall benefit in performance in the current dataset.
source: However, TMR in REM sleep lead to no overall benefit in performance in either our current dataset (Koopman et al., 2020) or previous studies (Rasch et al., 2007; Cordi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis and is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TMR in REM sleep lead to no overall benefit in performance in previous studies.
source: However, TMR in REM sleep lead to no overall benefit in performance in either our current dataset (Koopman et al., 2020) or previous studies (Rasch et al., 2007; Cordi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Examination of natural (un-cued) sleep showed a correlation between overnight memory improvement and the extent of memory-linked activity identified in non-REM but not REM sleep.
source: Furthermore, examination of natural (un-cued) sleep showed a correlation between overnight memory improvement and the extent of memory-linked activity identified in non-REM but not REM sleep (Schönauer et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There may be a difference in the function of replay in non-REM and REM sleep stages.
source: potentially suggesting a difference in the function of replay in these two sleep stages.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior research.

claim: The connection between hippocampus and neocortex is inhibited by the high levels of acetylcholine that are present in REM.
source: We are at a very early phase in understanding what TMR does in REM sleep, however we do know that the connection between hippocampus and neocortex is inhibited by the high levels of acetylcholine that are present in REM (Hasselmo, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The reactivation observed in the cortex is unlikely to be linked to corresponding hippocampal reactivation.
source: This means that the reactivation which we observe in the cortex is unlikely to be linked to corresponding hippocampal reactivation, so any consolidation which occurs as a result of this is also unlikely to be linked to the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior knowledge about acetylcholine in REM.

claim: Any consolidation which occurs as a result of reactivation in REM is unlikely to be linked to the hippocampus.
source: This means that the reactivation which we observe in the cortex is unlikely to be linked to corresponding hippocampal reactivation, so any consolidation which occurs as a result of this is also unlikely to be linked to the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior knowledge about acetylcholine in REM.

claim: The SRTT is a sequencing task which relies heavily on the hippocampus.
source: The SRTT is a sequencing task which relies heavily on the hippocampus, and our primary behavioural measure (sequence-specific skill [SSS]) specifically examines the sequencing element of the task.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the SRTT.

claim: TMR in non-REM sleep leads to extensive plasticity in the medial temporal lobe.
source: Our own neuroimaging work has shown that TMR in non-REM sleep leads to extensive plasticity in the medial temporal lobe (Cousins et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: If TMR in REM sleep has no impact on the hippocampus then it is possible that it elicits cortical reactivation and leads to cortical plasticity but provides no measurable benefit to SSS.
source: However, if TMR in REM sleep has no impact on the hippocampus then it is quite possible that it elicits cortical reactivation and leads to cortical plasticity but provides no measurable benefit to SSS.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: It is possible that behavioural improvements would have emerged several days later.
source: Alternatively, because we only measured behavioural improvement right after sleep it is possible that we may have missed behavioural improvements that would have emerged several days later, as we know can occur in this task (Rakowska et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The relatively low number of participants (n=14) is a limitation to the correlation analysis.
source: We should also mention our relatively low number of participants (n=14) is a limitation to this correlation and we recommend that future studies confirm the same relationship.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: TMR-locked reactivation in REM is delayed compared to wake after cue onset, similar to non-REM.
source: For instance, similar to non-REM (Cairney et al., 2018), TMR-locked reactivation in REM is delayed compared to wake after cue onset.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis compared to prior research.

claim: The reactivations detected appear to occur in roughly the same area of the cortex as is used in performing the task.
source: Furthermore, the reactivations we were able to detect appear to occur in roughly the same area of the cortex as is used in performing the task, and the extracted features of reactivation are similar to those extracted during wake activation which is why it is detectable using our machine learning models.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis.

claim: The extracted features of reactivation are similar to those extracted during wake activation.
source: Furthermore, the reactivations we were able to detect appear to occur in roughly the same area of the cortex as is used in performing the task, and the extracted features of reactivation are similar to those extracted during wake activation which is why it is detectable using our machine learning models.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis.

claim: An adaptation night was used to ensure that classification results from the experimental night were not caused by responses to sounds alone.
source: Firstly, we use an adaptation night, during which participants heard the TMR sounds before these were paired with any memory to ensure that our classification results from the experimental night were not caused by responses to sounds alone.
evidence: This describes the methodological control used in the study.

claim: The neural fingerprint associated with reactivation of a memory was captured using the EEG pattern occurring after TMR cues in sleep.
source: Secondly, in developing our classifier, we captured the neural fingerprint associated with reactivation of a memory using the EEG pattern occurring after TMR cues in sleep.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: The neural fingerprint was directly related to the pattern of brain activity during wakeful imagining of the task.
source: We then directly related this to the pattern of brain activity during wakeful imagining of the task.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: Training classification models on sleep EEG and testing them on wakeful imagining ensured that classification stems from memory reinstatement.
source: This was achieved by training our classification models on sleep EEG and testing them on wakeful imagining. Together, these procedures ensured that our classification stems from memory reinstatement and is related to genuine re-processing of memories during sleep.
evidence: This is a methodological rationale.

claim: The work builds on other studies showing discriminability of cued categories in sleep data without the inclusion of wake.
source: Our work builds on other studies showing discriminability of cued categories in sleep data without the inclusion of wake (Cairney et al., 2018; Schönauer et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The work builds on an approach that includes only the features that caused category discrimination in wake.
source: as well as on an approach that includes only the features that caused category discrimination in wake (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Classifiers trained with sleep are more robust in decoding the elicited reactivation than classifiers trained with wake.
source: We have explicitly examined the differential impact of training our classifiers with wake and training them with sleep and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 that the classifiers trained with sleep are more robust in decoding the elicited reactivation.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Future studies should adopt a similar approach by allowing the models to train on sleep data.
source: We therefore recommend that future studies adopt a similar approach by allowing the models to train on sleep data.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: REM reactivation has been suggested by modelling.
source: REM reactivation has been suggested by modelling (Hasselmo, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Evidence of learning-dependent activation in human REM sleep has been observed.
source: and evidence of learning-dependent activation in human REM sleep has been observed (Maquet et al., 2000; Peigneux et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Null behavioural findings from human REM TMR studies have led to scepticism amongst sleep researchers.
source: However, null behavioural findings from human REM TMR studies Rasch and Born, 2013; Rasch et al., 2007 have led to scepticism amongst sleep researchers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and reflects the state of the field.

claim: The current findings provide clear evidence that TMR in REM can elicit detectable reactivation.
source: Our current findings provide clear evidence that TMR in REM can elicit detectable reactivation.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: The analysis uncovers several important properties of REM reactivation, showing strong parallels with reactivation in non-REM sleep.
source: Furthermore, our analysis uncovers several important properties of REM reactivation, showing strong parallels with reactivation in non-REM sleep.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: More work is needed to explore how reactivation links to behavioural and neural plasticity.
source: More work is needed to explore how such reactivation links to behavioural and neural plasticity, and how this differs across a variety of cognitive tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: EEG and behavioural data were collected from 16 human participants.
source: EEG and behavioural data were collected from human participants (n=16) (8 females, 8 males, and age mean: 23.6).
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: Two participants were excluded due to technical problems.
source: Two participants were excluded due to technical problems, the rest of the datasets were included in the analyses (n=14).
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, normal hearing, and no history of physical, psychological, neurological, or sleep disorders.
source: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, normal hearing, and no history of physical, psychological, neurological, or sleep disorders.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Participants reported no stressful events, a regular sleep-wake rhythm in the month before the study, and no night work or cross-continental travel in the 2 months before the study.
source: Responses in pre-screening questionnaires reported no stressful events, a regular sleep-wake rhythm in the month before the study, and no night work or cross-continental travel in the 2 months before the study.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: All participants reported non-familiarity with the SRTT and all of them were right-handed.
source: All participants reported non-familiarity with the SRTT and all of them were right-handed.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Participants did not consume alcohol in the 24 hr before the study or caffeine in the 12 hr prior to the study or perform any extreme physical exercise or nap.
source: Participants did not consume alcohol in the 24 hr before the study or caffeine in the 12 hr prior to the study or perform any extreme physical exercise or nap.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Participants performed SRTT before and after sleep.
source: The SRTT was adapted from Cousins et al., 2014, and participants performed SRTT before and after sleep.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: During wakeful encoding, participants learned two 12-item sequences, A and B.
source: During wakeful encoding, participants learned two 12-item sequences, A and B, A: 1 2 1 4 2 3 4 1 3 2 4 3 and B: 2 4 3 2 3 1 4 2 3 1 4 1.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Sequences had been matched for learning difficulty; both contained each item three times.
source: Sequences had been matched for learning difficulty; both contained each item three times.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: There were 24 blocks of each sequence (48 blocks in total).
source: There were 24 blocks of each sequence (48 blocks in total), after each block a 15 s pause which could be extended by participants if they wish, during the pause participants were informed of their reaction time and error rate for the last block.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Two sets of pure musical tones were used, one consisted of low tones within the fourth octave (C/D/E/F) and the second consisted of high tones within the fifth octave (A/B/C#/D).
source: We used two sets of pure musical tones, one consisted of low tones within the fourth octave (C/D/E/F) and the second consisted of high tones within the fifth octave (A/B/C#/D).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each sequence was paired with either low tones or high tones.
source: Each sequence was paired with either low tones or high tones.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The 48 blocks of sequences A and B were followed by four blocks that contained random sequences.
source: The 48 blocks of sequences A and B were followed by four blocks that contained random sequences, which were used to help us isolate improvements in reaction time which were specific to sequence learning.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants were asked to sleep in the lab before doing the SRTT training as a control.
source: As a control, participants were asked to sleep in the lab before doing the SRTT training.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The control night followed the same criteria as the actual experiment with the difference that the sounds were not yet associated with any task.
source: The control night followed the same criteria as the actual experiment with the difference that the sounds were not yet associated with any task.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants performed the task again in the morning, first motor imagery then SRTT.
source: Participants performed the task again in the morning but this time they did first motor imagery then SRTT.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants were asked to try to remember the locations of the images of the two sequences to test their recall for each of the sequences.
source: They were then asked to try to remember the locations of the images of the two sequences to test their recall for each of the sequences.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Cues were delivered to participants during stable REM sleep which was identified using standard AASM criteria.
source: Cues were delivered to participants during stable REM sleep which was identified using standard American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) criteria (Richard et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Tones were presented in the correct order for the sequence, with a pause of 1500 ms in between tones in a sequence, and a 20 s break at the end of each sequence.
source: Tones were presented in the correct order for our sequence, with a pause of 1500 ms in between tones in a sequence, and a 20 s break at the end of each sequence.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: If participants showed any signs of arousal, or left REM sleep, cueing was paused immediately.
source: If participants showed any signs of arousal, or left REM sleep, cueing was paused immediately.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: EEG signals were acquired from 21 electrodes, following the 10–20 system.
source: EEG signals were acquired from 21 electrodes, following the 10–20 system.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition method.

claim: Electrodes were referenced to the mean of the left and right mastoid electrodes.
source: Electrodes were referenced to the mean of the left and right mastoid electrodes.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition method.

claim: The impedance was <5 kΩ for each scalp electrode, and <10 kΩ for each face electrode.
source: The impedance was <5 kΩ for each scalp electrode, and <10 kΩ for each face electrode.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition method.

claim: PSG recordings were scored by trained sleep scorers and only the segments scored as REM sleep were kept for further analyses.
source: PSG recordings were scored by trained sleep scorers and only the segments scored as REM sleep were kept for further analyses.
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: Data were collected at 200 Hz sampling rate.
source: Data were collected at 200 Hz sampling rate.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition method.

claim: EEG signals were band-pass filtered in the frequency range from 0.1 to 50 Hz.
source: EEG signals were band-pass filtered in the frequency range from (0.1 to 50 Hz).
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: Trials were segmented –0.5 s to 3 s relative to the onset of the cue.
source: Trials were segmented –0.5 s to 3 s relative to the onset of the cue.
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: 9.8% of trials were considered outliers and removed from the experimental night data.
source: Thus, 9.8% and 10.5% of trials were considered outliers and removed from the experimental night data and the adaptation night, respectively.
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: 10.5% of trials were considered outliers and removed from the adaptation night data.
source: Thus, 9.8% and 10.5% of trials were considered outliers and removed from the experimental night data and the adaptation night, respectively.
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: Data was analysed with independent component analysis (ICA) to remove eye movement artefacts.
source: Data was subsequently analysed with independent component analysis (ICA), to remove eye movement artefacts which can occur during REM.
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: Components identified by the ICA that were significantly correlated with the signals from the eye electrodes were removed.
source: Components identified by the ICA that were significantly correlated with the signals from the eye electrodes (corrected for multiple comparisons) were removed.
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: A hanning taper with 5 cycles was used for time-frequency analysis.
source: Our time-frequency analysis used a similar method to that used in Cairney et al., 2018. We used a hanning taper with 5 cycles that was convolved with the signals.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: 0.5 Hz frequency steps and 5 ms time steps were used in time-frequency analysis.
source: We used 0.5 Hz frequency steps and 5 ms time steps.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: A baseline of –300 ms to –100 ms pre-stimulus was used in time-frequency analysis.
source: We also used a similar baseline of –300 ms to –100 ms pre-stimulus.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: The reported values in time-frequency analysis represent the percentage of power change from baseline.
source: The reported values represent the percentage of power change from baseline.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: A baseline period of –200 ms to 0 ms was used for ERP analysis.
source: For the ERP analysis, we adopted a similar approach to that in Cairney et al., 2018. We identified a baseline period of –200 ms to 0 ms and we reported the grand average from all participants and all channels.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: EEG signals were smoothed using 100 ms window in time × time classification.
source: We first smoothed the EEG signals using 100 ms window such that every time point was replaced with the average of the 50 ms of both sides around it.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: A searchlight analysis used data from 12 participants who had performed the same SRTT task but had not undergone REM TMR.
source: We used a searchlight analysis to locate channels of interest. This used data from 12 participants who had performed the same SRTT task as those in the current study, but who had not undergone REM TMR and were therefore not included in our current dataset.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: The classification used the smoothed amplitudes as features and LDA classifiers with fivefold cross-validation.
source: Our classification used the smoothed amplitudes as features and LDA classifiers with fivefold cross-validation.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Trial length was 1.5 s in sleep and 1.1 s in wake.
source: The process was then repeated for all time points after a sound cue in sleep (trial length was: 1.5 s in sleep and 1.1 s in wake).
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Classifiers were first trained on sleep data from a participant and tested on wake data from that same participant, then the AUC values from different participants were averaged.
source: Classifiers were first trained on sleep data from a participant and tested on wake data from that same participant, then the AUC values from different participants were averaged.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: In sleep, only sounds from the cued sequence were used.
source: In sleep, only sounds from the cued sequence were used.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Motor imagery data from both cued and un-cued sequences and from both pre-and post-sleep imagery sessions were included when testing the classifier on wake data.
source: When testing the classifier on wake data, we were interested in the differential activation pattern for left- and right-handed motor imagery. We therefore included motor imagery data from both cued and un-cued sequences and from both pre-and post-sleep imagery sessions.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: For one participant, only the post-sleep imagery was used due to an issue with the recorded data of pre-sleep imagery.
source: There was an issue with the recorded data of pre-sleep imagery for one participant, thus, for that participant only the post-sleep imagery was used.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Fidelity of TMR response was incorporated in the model by measuring the average theta power at [4 8]Hz in the first second after TMR.
source: We thus incorporated fidelity of TMR response to this pattern in our model. We did this by measuring the average theta power at [4 8]Hz in the first second after TMR.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Values that were higher than the 90th percentile were set to 1 and those lower than the 10th percentile were set to 0 when weighting trials.
source: Values that were higher than the 90th percentile were set to 1 and those lower than the 10th percentile were set to 0, with normalisation and flooring and capping weights reflect the fidelity of each TMR cue.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: The AUC was used as the performance measure in classification.
source: We used the AUC as the performance measure in our classification.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: The clustering window used for cluster-based permutation was the whole length of trials.
source: The clustering window used for cluster-based permutation was the whole length of trials (i.e., the whole time × time classification duration) which gave a stringent test.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: The average of the best four blocks before and after sleep was taken to calculate performance.
source: The most robust measure of performance on the SRTT comes from the best performance blocks in each session (Cousins et al., 2014), we therefore took the average of the best four blocks before and after sleep to calculate performance.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Sequence-specific skill (SSS) is the SRTT measure which consolidates most strongly with sleep.
source: The SRTT measure which consolidates most strongly with sleep (Spencer et al., 2006) and with TMR (Cousins et al., 2014; Cousins et al., 2016) is SSS.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SSS was calculated by subtracting reaction times on sequenced blocks from reaction times on the associated random blocks.
source: This was calculated by subtracting reaction times on sequenced blocks from reaction times on the associated random blocks: SSS = (mean of random blocks – mean of best four blocks).
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Behavioural improvement across sleep was calculated by: (SSS post-sleep – SSS pre-sleep)/SSS pre-sleep.
source: Behavioural improvement across sleep was then calculated by: (SSS post-sleep – SSS pre-sleep)/SSS pre-sleep.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Relative sequence improvement (cued vs un-cued) was calculated as: (improvement across sleep of the cued sequence – improvement across sleep of the un-cued sequence)/improvement across sleep of the un-cued sequence.
source: In order to determine whether there are differences in this measure as a result of TMR, we calculated the relative difference in overnight improvement for cued and un-cued sequences as follows: relative sequence improvement (cued vs un-cued) = (improvement across sleep of the cued sequence – improvement across sleep of the un-cued sequence)/improvement across sleep of the un-cued sequence.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Classification performance was calculated as the mean of classification AUC values from each participant inside the cluster when correlating with relative cued vs. un-cued sequence improvement.
source: When we correlated the relative cued vs. un-cued sequence improvement with classification performance, we calculated the latter as the mean of classification AUC values from each participant inside the cluster shown in Figure 2c.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Cluster-based permutation with sample-specific threshold of 0.05 was used for multiple comparisons correction.
source: Cluster-based permutation with sample-specific threshold of 0.05 was used.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: Permutation test threshold for clusters was 0.05.
source: Permutation test threshold for clusters was 0.05.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.
